reasons: The scoring logic, defaults and presets are not in this review.

terms.meaning: a label that tells the code editor which shape of data to expect, so mistakes are caught early
a number that sets how much one factor counts toward the final score
the final number from 0 to 100 that ranks a signal

used_by: artifacts/capital-projects/src/tools/opportunity-map/index.tsx (passes weights to the priority view; the import is not visible in this packet)

sections.name: File setup, Factor, Weights
sections.title: Factor names and weight type
sections.what: Lists the nine factors an analyst can weigh: value, severity, urgency, solution fit, ability to act, evidence, capex, strength and focus. It also defines the type that holds one weight per factor.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed list of names keeps every screen using the same factors.
sections.watch_out: Any place that uses a factor name must match these spellings exactly, or that factor will not be found.

sections.name: FACTORS, DEFAULT_WEIGHTS
sections.title: Priority factors and default weights
sections.what: Lists the nine factors used to rank opportunities, each with a short hint shown to users, and sets the starting importance (weight) of each. The default weights add up to 110, not 100.
sections.why: The hints explain each factor to the user, and the default weights give the starting balance of the score.
sections.watch_out: The score divides by the total of the weights, so the total does not need to be 100, but each factor key must match the Factor type exactly.

sections.name: PRESETS
sections.title: Named weight presets
sections.what: Provides four ready-made weight sets: Balanced (the default), Capex-led, Act now, and Best evidenced. Each one puts more importance on a different goal.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets users switch the ranking focus in one step without setting nine weights by hand.
sections.watch_out: The Balanced preset reuses the default weights object, so changing the defaults also changes that preset.

sections.name: loadWeights, sameWeights
sections.title: Loading and comparing saved weights
sections.what: Reads the user's saved weights from browser storage and uses them only if every factor has a value from 0 to 100. Otherwise it uses the defaults. Also provides a check for whether two weight sets are the same.
sections.why: Stated in the code: weights saved before a new factor existed keep their values, and the new factor takes its default.
sections.watch_out: The storage key includes a version suffix, so changing the shape of the saved weights requires a new version or old saved data may be misread.

sections.name: CAPEX_BANDS, CapexBand
sections.title: Project capex size bands
sections.what: Defines four size bands for a project's capital cost, from megaproject (one billion US dollars or more) down to small (under 100 million), each with a rating from 5 down to 2. Also defines the band types, including plan and unknown.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the labels and ratings.
sections.watch_out: The bands are checked in order from largest to smallest, so changing their order changes which band a project falls into.

sections.name: capexBand
sections.title: Choosing a project's capex band
sections.what: Works out which size band a project's capital cost falls into. A project with no cost figure is unknown, and a company-wide plan is placed in its own group.
sections.why: Stated in the code: company-wide capex plans are not project capex, so they do not raise the priority.
sections.watch_out: A project is treated as a company plan only when its scope is marked that way, so a mislabelled plan would be ranked as a project and raise its priority.

sections.name: CAPEX_BAND_LABEL, capexRating, EVIDENCE
sections.title: Labels and evidence scores
sections.what: Holds the readable label for each capex band, a function that turns a project's band into a 1 to 5 rating (unknown scores 1), and a table that gives each evidence grade C1 to C4 a score.
sections.why: Reason for the specific evidence scores is not stated in the code. The grade table suggests that official, direct evidence counts more.
sections.watch_out: An evidence grade missing from the table quietly scores 1, so a typing mistake in a grade makes a project look weakly evidenced.

sections.name: ratings
sections.title: Building all factor ratings for a project
sections.what: Gives every factor a 1 to 5 rating for one project. Uses the mapped score when present, falls back to a value based on the older overall priority when not, scales the signal strength score, and turns the focus adjustment into a 1 to 5 rating around 3.
sections.why: Likely reason: every factor needs a comparable number before the weights can be applied.
sections.watch_out: Projects missing mapped scores get a fallback that depends on the older overall priority, so their ratings change if that value changes.

sections.name: customScore
sections.title: Overall custom score
sections.what: Combines the nine factor ratings into one score from 0 to 100, using the current weights as the importance of each. Returns 0 when every weight is zero.
sections.why: Lets the score follow the user's own weights rather than a fixed formula.
sections.watch_out: The score assumes each rating is from 1 to 5, so a rating outside that range will push the final score outside 0 to 100.

sections.name: axes
sections.title: Impact and actionability positions
sections.what: Splits the factor ratings into two positions: impact (capex, value, severity) and actionability (urgency, solution fit, ability to act, evidence, strength and focus). Each is a 1 to 5 value, weighted by the current weights.
sections.why: The code comment defines impact as how much is at stake and actionability as how ready the opportunity is to pursue.
sections.watch_out: Changing the weights can move a project's position on the map even when nothing about the project has changed.

summary: Names the nine factors an analyst can weigh when ranking opportunities and defines the type that holds their weights.
purpose: Lets an analyst decide how much each factor counts, so that signals can be ranked on a score from 0 to 100.
why: Likely reason: a shared list of factor names keeps the priority screen and the ranking code in agreement. Otherwise not stated in the code.
how: Each factor gets a rating from 1 to 5 for a signal. The weight for each factor sets how much it counts. According to the file comment, these combine into one score from 0 to 100. Only the first five lines were in this review, so the combining step is not checked here.
inputs: The analyst's weight for each factor, and the signal's ratings and details, typed as Opportunity and OmCapex from omApi.ts.
outputs: A list of factor names and a weight type used across the file. The 0 to 100 score is described in a comment but is produced by code that is not in this review.
risks: Renaming a factor breaks every place that uses the old name, and not all of those places are visible here. Adding a factor needs a matching weight, default and rating in each place that lists factors.
debug: If the ranking looks wrong, check that factor names match exactly on every screen and in the default weights. Confirm each weight is a number and each rating is between 1 and 5. The defaults, presets and scoring code were not in this review, so check them in the file itself.
